answer:
Pick **the dental appointment-setting service**, initially focused on converting existing inquiries into attended appointments. Your front-desk experience gives you an advantage; generating leads through advertising requires additional skills.

The store would leave only $5,000 before marketing and operating costs. Vending would leave $2,000, while its unverified $700 monthly profit falls well short of your goal.

Keep your job. Protect at least $8,700 as an emergency reserve—three months of expenses—and cap initial spending at $1,000. Your $500 monthly surplus can fund further testing.

- **Days 1–30:** Interview 15 practice owners or managers. Find offices with unconverted inquiries and available appointment capacity. Offer scheduled evening or weekend follow-up during hours you can reliably cover. Check employment restrictions; use no employer patient data, equipment, or work time. Establish appropriate patient-data agreements, secure access, and communication consent before delivery. Seek one paid pilot.
- **Days 31–60:** Run two tightly scoped, 30-day pilots. Test a $750–$1,000 fixed fee with defined inquiry volume and coverage hours. Track baseline conversion, bookings, attendance, incremental practice profit, and your delivery time. Avoid revenue guarantees.
- **Days 61–90:** Seek renewals at a sustainable monthly price, document your process, and acquire a third client through direct outreach. Allocate roughly six weekly hours to sales, twelve to delivery, and two to administration.

For illustration, five clients paying $1,500 produce $7,500 revenue; subtract delivery costs, overhead, taxes, and replacement benefits before comparing it with your $3,400 take-home.

Continue if clients renew, their incremental profit comfortably exceeds your fee, and delivery fits 20 hours. Otherwise revise scope or pricing before expanding. Treat 18 months as a target; quit only after six months of reliable replacement income and a six-month personal reserve.
